sources.citation: Kamholz, David C. 2014. Austronesians in Papua: Diversification and change in South Halmahera-West New Guinea. PhD dissertation, UC Berkeley.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Busami data are second-hand (Silzer 1983). Sec. 5.4 reconstructs penultimate stress for Proto-SHWNG from descriptions of Buli, Sawai, Taba, Ambai, Wandamen, Waropen, Warembori; Busami is not among the languages with any stress description. p. 38 reports Price & Donohue (2008 ms) claim that 'other languages of Yapen also have complex stress systems' without Busami specifics.

sources.citation: Silzer, Peter J. 1983. Ambai: an Austronesian language of Irian Jaya, Indonesia. PhD thesis, Australian National University.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No Busami phonology. Busami appears in the lexicostatistic table and in Appendix A pp. 237-238, where Silzer says the two Ambai verb-stem stress classes 'are also present in the other [Yapen] languages. All Yapen languages, except Busami, exhibit different patterns of interaction between the infixes /-u-/ and /-i-/ with verbs with the initial syllable of the stem stressed and those with the initial syllable of the verb unstressed' -- an oblique remark, not a statement of where Busami word stress falls.

sources.citation: Anceaux, J.C. 1961. The linguistic situation in the islands of Yapen, Kurudu, Nau and Miosnum, New Guinea. Verhandelingen KITLV 35. 's-Gravenhage: Martinus Nijhoff. 166 pp. (OAPEN open access, DOI 10.26530/oapen_613371)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Busami stress. Busami = section J, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 16): 'It is to be regretted that only scant information could be collected about this language'. Transcription note printed p. 14 (PDF p. 22): 'Stress-accent, vowel pitch and vowel length (part of the accentual system in many of these languages) are not indicated.' The book's only accent remark concerns Papuma (p. 7). Busami forms appear unaccented throughout the comparative word-list and correspondence sets.
